items.good: The README has the template's headings in its order: the name, an opening under no heading, Example, Why organize-downloads, Requirements, Installation, Documentation, Development, License. The opening's first sentence gives the idea (one folder per kind chosen by extension, a list of moves before any move, no file deleted, renamed or overwritten, an undo); its second gives the kind of thing (a command-line tool for macOS and Linux), whom it is for and the gain (finding the file in a folder of its kind). Each section opens with its main point. Each list item in Why, Requirements and Documentation is one sentence that reads alone, with its explanation after a blank line and indented under it, and no item is in bold.

From the opening I know what the tool does and how it differs from tidying by hand: it picks the folder for each file itself by its extension, shows every move before making any, never deletes, renames or overwrites, and can undo. It also says what the tool is (a command-line tool for macOS and Linux), whom it is for (someone whose Downloads folder holds so many files they cannot find the one they want) and what they gain (finding that file in a folder of its kind). A reader with a crowded Downloads folder can tell it is for them.

The example is a Downloads folder like a reader's own, with the awkward cases in it: a hidden file, an unfinished download, a file with no extension, a name already taken in Documents, and a folder of the user's own. It follows the three runs in the order I would make them, and shows what each gives back: the lines printed with no option, the folder tree after --move, the lines printed by --undo, and that the folder is then as it was at first. Every turn is the reader running a command and the tool answering, told in that order.

Why compares the tool with the three other ways of doing the same work, and each point is something this tool does that the other way leaves to me: by hand I make every folder and drag every file; sorting by kind in Finder or Files changes only the view, and the files stay in one folder; a rule-based organizer needs me to write rules first, while this tool comes with its kinds already set. None of the points is a benefit that every way gives.

parts.good: Each sentence makes sense on its own. 'Kind of file' is explained in the same sentence where it first appears, as chosen by the file's extension, and nothing depends on a later section.

The starting folder, each command and its output, and the folder after each run are shown in blocks, in the order they happen. Why two files get no line is explained right after the output. The undo cases that fail are named together with what happens in them. The extension rule is explained, with archive.tar.gz as an example, before the table, and the kinds are laid out in a table.

Each other way is named so I can recognise it (Finder, Files, an organizer that sorts by rules), with what it leaves undone in the same sentence. The point about built-in kinds refers back to the table I have already read.

Each requirement says what it is, then why it is needed and how to check it, with each command in its own block, including the new Linux Python install. The PATH step tells me which startup file to use for which shell, and the command that shows the shell comes before the line to add.
The install commands are in one block, followed by the check command, then the first use, which points back to the Example I have already read, then the macOS permission prompt and what to answer.
Each item says what I will find and where it is.
One sentence says what the linked page holds: how the tool is made and how its tests are run.
It names the license and links to its text.
This is the standard MIT license text, with the year and holder in the copyright line, and it reads straight through.

items.good: Each part tells me something no other part does. The opening gives the idea and the gain, and Why gives only the comparison with other ways, without repeating the gain. The Example shows the runs once, and Installation points back to them instead of repeating them. The --move output is not printed a second time. The table, the default folder, the undo cases that fail and the rule that your own folders are left alone each appear once. The Python and curl install lines each say only how to get their own thing. Nothing is written for a reviewer, and nothing tells how a decision was reached.

So I cannot rely on the claims about what it prints, what it moves and leaves, that it works with Python 3.8 or later, that it works on macOS, or that --help prints how to run it.
